terms.definition: A unit of data passed between systems, such as "order 42 was placed".
A producer sends messages; a consumer reads and processes them.
Add to the end of something without changing what is already there.

before.note: Read Message Queues first: a queue removes a message once it is handled, and a log is what you get when it stays. Pub-Sub and Replication also help, but the terms above are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: A message queue hands each message to one consumer and then forgets it. A log keeps messages in the order they were written and lets any number of readers go through them, each at its own pace. The Kafka documentation describes event streaming as capturing events as they happen, storing them durably for later, processing them as they occur or afterwards, and routing them to other systems [[kafka-intro]].

In Kafka the unit is the event, also called a record or message. Events are kept in topics, which the docs compare to a folder in a file system, with events as the files. A topic can have zero, one or many producers and consumers, and unlike traditional messaging, events are not deleted after they are consumed. You set per topic how long to retain them [[kafka-intro]].

terms.definition: A record that something happened, with a key, a value and a timestamp [[kafka-intro]].
A named place events are written to and read from; many producers and many consumers can share one [[kafka-intro]].
A per-topic setting for how long events are kept before old ones are discarded [[kafka-intro]].

stages.name: How it works
body: A topic is divided into partitions that live on different brokers, so many clients can read and write at once. Events with the same key go to the same partition, and Kafka guarantees that a consumer of a partition reads its events in the order they were written [[kafka-intro]]. There is no such promise across partitions.

On disk a partition is a directory of log files. Each message is identified by a 64-bit offset, and each file is named after the offset of its first message [[kafka-log]]. A consumer fetches from an offset and gets back a chunk of log, and it can rewind to re-consume data [[kafka-design]].

Because each partition is read by exactly one consumer in a consumer group at a time, a consumer's position in a partition is a single integer, the offset of the next message to read. The docs call this state very small and say it can be checkpointed [[kafka-design]].

Every partition has one leader and zero or more followers. All writes go to the leader, and followers copy its log [[kafka-design]]. The docs note a replication factor of 3 as a common production setting [[kafka-intro]].

terms.definition: One ordered slice of a topic, placed on a broker [[kafka-intro]].
A message's position in its partition [[kafka-log]].
Consumers that share a topic, with each partition read by one member at a time [[kafka-design]].
The leader of a partition takes writes, and the followers copy it [[kafka-design]].

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Kafka relies on the file system and the operating system's page cache instead of keeping a cache of its own. Its design page argues that linear reads and writes are the most predictable pattern and well optimised by the OS, and that appending to a file keeps operations at constant cost whatever the data size [[kafka-design]]. That is why it can keep messages for a long time, for example a week [[kafka-design]].

Deletion happens one log segment at a time, by age or by size [[kafka-log]]. Log compaction is a different kind of retention: it removes records whose key has a newer record, so the log keeps at least the final state of every key, in order, and offsets never change [[kafka-design]].

Delivery is at-least-once by default. Committing offsets before processing gives at-most-once, and Kafka's transactions can give exactly-once between topics by writing the output and the consumer's offset together [[kafka-design]].

terms.definition: One file of a partition's log; the oldest segments are deleted first [[kafka-log]].
Retention that keeps the latest record for each key [[kafka-design]].
A message may be delivered more than once, but is not lost; Kafka's default [[kafka-design]].

reading.what: Why a disk log is fast enough, and what compaction guarantees.
What at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once mean for a consumer that commits offsets.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: The Kafka use cases page lists messaging, website activity tracking, metrics, log aggregation, stream processing, event sourcing and a commit log for other systems [[kafka-uses]]. Kafka Connect can run connectors that move data in and out of other systems, such as a connector that captures every change to a set of PostgreSQL tables [[kafka-intro]].

Durability and availability pull against each other. A producer can wait for 0, 1 or all in-sync replicas, and a minimum in-sync set can make a partition refuse writes it could not protect. The docs describe this as a trade-off between consistency and availability, and the choice of whether an out-of-sync replica may become leader is the same trade-off [[kafka-design]].

Retention is a cost choice. Keeping more lets a consumer rewind further or a new consumer start from the beginning, and it takes more disk. The Uber paper on the topic page shows the other side of the choice: Uber keeps Kafka retention to a few days and replays older data from archives.

terms.definition: A follower that is caught up with the leader; writes count as safe once those have them [[kafka-design]].
Tooling for connectors that import and export data between Kafka and other systems [[kafka-intro]].

misconceptions.myth: A log-based system is a queue with a different name.
misconceptions.truth: A queue is built around removing messages once they are handled. In Kafka, events are not deleted after consumption, and a consumer can rewind to an old offset and read again [[kafka-intro]] [[kafka-design]].

misconceptions.myth: All events in a topic are in one global order.
misconceptions.truth: Order is guaranteed within a partition. Events with the same key go to the same partition, but different partitions have no shared order [[kafka-intro]].
Retention is a per-topic setting after which old events are discarded, and compaction keeps only the latest record per key [[kafka-intro]] [[kafka-design]].

misconceptions.myth: The broker must remember which messages each consumer has handled.
misconceptions.truth: In Kafka a consumer's position per partition is just one integer, which makes the bookkeeping very small [[kafka-design]].

They come from the Kafka quickstart, with its example topic quickstart-events, which the page shows with Kafka 4.3.1 and a local Java 17 or newer. The page shows its own output; yours depends on your cluster.
